Escalate locally, or collect what is accessible as that user
Use the host as a staging point for the next hop

remediation.step: Enumerate the three groups across the estate, looking for broad principals like Domain Users or Authenticated Users.
remediation.command: Invoke-Command -ComputerName SERVER01 -ScriptBlock { 'Remote Desktop Users','Remote Management Users','Distributed COM Users' | ForEach-Object { Get-LocalGroupMember -Group $_ -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue } }

remediation.step: Replace broad membership with the specific group that needs access to that specific host, managed by Group Policy rather than locally.
Restrict WinRM and RDP at the network layer so they are reachable only from administrative subnets or jump hosts, not from any workstation.
Verify that your application control policy covers script execution arriving over WinRM, not only interactive execution. Several products have a gap here that is easy to assume away.
Enable PowerShell script block logging and module logging so remote execution is recorded regardless of the channel used.
remediation.command: # Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging

breakRisk: Tightening RDP or WinRM membership will cut off users who quietly depended on it, including automation that connects with a service account. Review recent logon events for each host before changing membership.
lab: Grant a low-privileged lab user CanPSRemote to a server and connect. Then check whether your endpoint tooling logged the session and whether application control applied to the commands you ran.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001 - Remote Desktop Protocol
MITRE ATT&CK T1021.006 - Windows Remote Management

title: SQLAdmin: sysadmin rights on a SQL Server instance
summary: A principal holds sysadmin on a SQL Server instance, which generally converts to code execution on the host as the service account.
howItWorks: SQL Server sysadmin is a path out of the database and onto the operating system. The classic route is enabling and calling xp_cmdshell, which executes as the SQL service account, but there are others including CLR assemblies and agent jobs. The severity depends on what that service account is: a domain account running SQL on several servers, or worse an account in Domain Admins, turns a database permission into domain compromise. Linked servers extend the reach further, because a sysadmin on one instance can often execute on another through the link.
attackChain: Compromise a principal with sysadmin on an instance
Enable and use xp_cmdshell, or deploy a CLR assembly, to run commands
Execute as the SQL service account on that host
Follow linked servers to other instances and repeat

remediation.step: Enumerate sysadmin membership on each instance and identify which logins are domain groups rather than individuals.
remediation.command: Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance SQL01 -Query "SELECT p.name, p.type_desc FROM sys.server_role_members rm JOIN sys.server_principals p ON rm.member_principal_id = p.principal_id JOIN sys.server_principals r ON rm.role_principal_id = r.principal_id WHERE r.name = 'sysadmin'"

remediation.step: Remove sysadmin from anyone who does not administer the database engine itself. Application accounts almost never need it.
remediation.command: Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance SQL01 -Query "ALTER SERVER ROLE sysadmin DROP MEMBER [CORP\AppTeam]"

remediation.step: Run the SQL service under a low-privileged account or a gMSA, never a domain administrator. This caps what a successful escalation reaches.
Confirm xp_cmdshell is disabled and CLR integration is off unless a documented application requires them.
remediation.command: Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance SQL01 -Query "EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options',1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell'"

remediation.step: Review linked servers and the credential context each one uses, since a link configured with a privileged account extends this path silently.

validation: Invoke-Sqlcmd -ServerInstance SQL01 -Query "SELECT p.name FROM sys.server_role_members rm JOIN sys.server_principals p ON rm.member_principal_id = p.principal_id JOIN sys.server_principals r ON rm.role_principal_id = r.principal_id WHERE r.name = 'sysadmin'"
breakRisk: Applications that were installed with sysadmin and never re-scoped will fail on operations they should not have been doing. Test in a non-production instance, since the permission the application actually needs is usually db_owner on one database.
lab: In a lab instance, use sysadmin to enable xp_cmdshell and run a command, then check which account it ran as. Change the service account and repeat to see the blast radius change.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1059 - Command and Scripting Interpreter

title: HasSIDHistory: privileged SID carried in an account's history
summary: An account's sIDHistory attribute contains the SID of another principal, so it receives that principal's access without being a member of anything.
howItWorks: sIDHistory exists so migrated accounts keep access to resources still permissioned to their old SID. The value is added to the user's token at logon, which means an account can hold administrative access with no group membership to show for it. That makes it both a legitimate migration artefact and an excellent persistence mechanism: an attacker who can write the attribute adds a privileged SID and gains that access invisibly to anyone reviewing group membership. Migrations that were never cleaned up leave the same exposure by accident, sometimes years later.
attackChain: Write a privileged SID into a controlled account's sIDHistory, or find an account that already carries one
Log on to receive the additional SID in the token
Access resources permissioned to the historical principal
Remain invisible to group membership reviews

remediation.step: Find every account carrying sIDHistory and resolve what each historical SID maps to.
Flag any historical SID whose RID indicates a privileged group, particularly 512, 516, 518, 519, and 520, plus the built-in administrators SID.
Re-permission the resources that still rely on the old SID, then clear the attribute. Clearing first will break access.
Enable SID filtering on trusts so a SID from another domain cannot be injected across the trust boundary.
Close out the migration formally. sIDHistory should be empty in a domain with no migration in progress, so treat any value as either unfinished work or an intrusion.

breakRisk: Clearing sIDHistory before re-permissioning breaks access to any resource still using the old SID, often file shares nobody has an inventory of. Re-permission first, verify, then clear.
lab: Add a privileged SID to a lab account's sIDHistory, log on, and run whoami /groups to see the SID appear in the token while the group membership list stays empty.
